title: Tunable Latent Generative Priors for Compressed Sensing and Inverse Problems
claim: Optimal model complexity is not the maximum: intermediate latent dimensionality minimizes error under few measurements, and the optimum shifts as data grows.
layout: 4 panels in a row, shared axes, dashed line marks optimum
description: Four side-by-side line plots share a y-axis (PSNR in dB, roughly 10 to 50) and an x-axis (latent dimension k, from 16 to 456). Each panel is a different measurement ratio. The panel titles are cropped at the top. Each panel shows blue dots joined by a line, with light-blue error bars. The best point is an orange dot with a dashed vertical orange line, and each panel has an 'optimal k = ...' label. In the first panel, PSNR peaks near k=64 at about 17 dB and then declines. In the second, it peaks at k=128 at about 22 dB and then drops at large k. In the third and fourth, PSNR rises steadily and peaks at k=456, reaching about 35 and 45 dB. The eye goes to the orange optimum markers, which move rightward from panel to panel.
caption: Intermediate latent dimensionalities yield the best reconstruction at low measurement ratios. Separate injective flow models (no parameter sharing) are trained for each latent dimensionality k ∈[16, 456] on MNIST (n = 32 × 32 = 1024). Each panel corresponds to a different measurement count m: for m < n, the forward operator is an m × n random Gaussian matrix (compressed sensing); note m = 1024 is the identity. Intermediate k (64 ≤k ≤200) minimizes reconstruction error at small m/n, with the optimal k shifting as m grows (error bars: ±1 std).
abstract: Latent generative models have emerged as powerful priors for solving inverse problems. These models typically represent a class of natural signals at a single, fixed complexity, governed by the latent dimensionality. This can be limiting: depending on the problem, a latent dimensionality that is too small may result in high representation error, while one that is too large may overfit to noise. We develop tunable latent priors for diffusion models, normalizing flows, and variational autoencoders, leveraging nested dropout. Across tasks including compressed sensing, inpainting, denoising, and phase retrieval, we show empirically that tunable priors consistently achieve lower reconstruction errors than fixed-complexity baselines. In the linear denoising setting, we derive the optimal complexity in closed form, showing how it depends on the noise level and the signal spectrum. This work demonstrates the potential of tunable latent generative priors and motivates both the development of supporting theory and their application across a wide range of inverse problems.
